item.title: Ro Teimumu highlights unfinished iTaukei reforms

item.content:encoded:
THE Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) remains at the centre of unfinished iTaukei reforms, with Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa saying the institution has yet to regain its “rightful position” under Fiji’s Constitution.

Speaking during an interview after the launch of the celebrating women in Parliament booklet earlier this week, Ro Teimumu said despite progress made by the Coalition Government in returning some land to traditional landowners, key reforms affecting iTaukei rights and institutions remained unresolved.

“To bring back the Great Council of Chiefs into its proper legislation, to enact it and to give autonomy,” she said.

She said the GCC’s restoration was not only about the institution itself, but also about recognising its historical role and contribution to Fiji’s governance.

“The FijiFirst Government decided that the way to do away with iTaukei rights to their resources was to chop from the top and that is why they targeted the Great Council of Chiefs.”

Ro Teimumu acknowledged that the Coalition Government had taken steps to address some of the concerns raised by iTaukei communities but said many issues could not be resolved within one term.

“What I’m talking about is the i qoliqoli, the land, the common name, and Bose Levu Vakaturaga.

“You cannot address everything in four years.”

She said the future of iTaukei institutions depended on continued efforts to ensure they had an effective role in Fiji’s development and decision-making.

item.title: Union seeks answers
item.description: THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) is questioning Government’s silence over the job evaluation exercise (JEE) program for teachers which would have resulted in salary readjustments for some. FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said the last JEE was carried out between 2017 and 2018 and failed to involve union representatives.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) is questioning Government’s silence over the job evaluation exercise (JEE) program for teachers which would have resulted in salary readjustments for some.

FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said the last JEE was carried out between 2017 and 2018 and failed to involve union representatives.

“A credible evaluation cannot be undertaken without the participation of the very people who understand the work, responsibilities and challenges of teachers,” he said.

“Teachers were given renewed hope when the former Minister for Finance announced in his 2024 Diwali message that a job evaluation exercise would be undertaken.

“That same message was repeated at the FTU annual general meeting by the chief guest on behalf of the Prime Minister, who indicated that the exercise would commence during the 2026-27 financial year. Unfortunately, the national budget was silent.

“Equally disappointing was the absence of any salary increase for teachers despite the growing cost of living and worsening teacher shortage.”

He said a JEE would ensure equal pay for work of equal value and recognise increased responsibilities of teachers working in a changing classroom environment.

“International good practice recommends that comprehensive public sector job evaluations be reviewed approximately every five to seven years, or sooner where there are significant changes in duties and workplace demands.

“Fiji’s teachers are now well overdue for such a review.

“Teachers have carried the education system through curriculum reforms, technological changes, increasing student welfare responsibilities and a severe teacher shortage.”

Questions sent to the Finance Ministry remain unanswered.

item.title: ‘UN still owes us’
item.description: PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the United Nations owes Fiji millions of dollars in financing their contribution to peacekeeping duties. While speaking after welcoming United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix at the Blackrock Camp in Nadi, Mr Rabuka said the visit offered an opportunity for Fiji to discuss their concerns about financing Fijian officers on
item.content:encoded:
PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the United Nations owes Fiji millions of dollars in financing their contribution to peacekeeping duties.

While speaking after welcoming United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix at the Blackrock Camp in Nadi, Mr Rabuka said the visit offered an opportunity for Fiji to discuss their concerns about financing Fijian officers on UN peacekeeping duties.

“It gives us an opportunity to see what we have at home in our capacity to keep abreast with developments and training.

“It is also an opportunity for me as Prime Minister to tell him about the impact and the burden of peacekeeping, particularly the financing of our contributions.

“The UN still owes us a few hundred million dollars, which could have gone into infrastructure development, particularly in health, transport and education.”

During the welcome ceremony, Mr Lacroix acknowledged Fiji’s contributions to the UN Peacekeeping movement.

“I assure you that this day will mark an important step in the common work that we do and that we will continue to do serving peace, serving humanity,” he said.

“Your commitment to being an active contributor to the safety and security of the whole region in the Pacific is also very valuable and appreciated and we are very much looking forward to working with you so that the voice of Fiji and indeed the voice of the Pacific region is being heard loudly in the efforts that we will continue to make.”

item.title: Singh returns to Sugar Ministry
item.description: Charan Jeath Singh is back as Sugar Minister after Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka reversed an earlier Cabinet allocation that placed the responsibility under Agriculture Minister Tomasi Tunabuna. Mr Singh confirmed the development yesterday, saying he was informed of the decision through an email from the Prime Minister on Monday night.
item.content:encoded:
Charan Jeath Singh is back as Sugar Minister after Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka reversed an earlier Cabinet allocation that placed the responsibility under Agriculture Minister Tomasi Tunabuna.

Mr Singh confirmed the development yesterday, saying he was informed of the decision through an email from the Prime Minister on Monday night.

“Now, I will be able to assist farmers more and will respect the decision of Mr Rabuka,” he said.

Mr Singh said he would formally take up the portfolio next week.

Mr Singh previously held the Sugar Industry portfolio before a Cabinet reshuffle several months ago which saw Mr Singh moved to Public Enterprises, Multi-Ethnic Affairs, Culture, Heritage and Arts.

Mr Singh’s return places him back at the centre of efforts to address challenges facing sugarcane farmers and the wider industry.

item.title: Scoping works for Lautoka pool set for August completion
item.description: THE revised scope of works of the yet to be completed Lautoka swimming pool could be completed by the end of August. The Lautoka City Council was forced to review the project plan after the Local Government Ministry’s submission for further funding under the 2026-2027 National Budget was rejected by the Finance Ministry.
item.content:encoded:
THE revised scope of works of the yet to be completed Lautoka swimming pool could be completed by the end of August.

The Lautoka City Council was forced to review the project plan after the Local Government Ministry’s submission for further funding under the 2026-2027 National Budget was rejected by the Finance Ministry.

Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel has since explained funding for the project, which received $1.9million last year, was redirected.

Lautoka City Council special administrators’ council chairperson Taitusi Rasoki said the new plan would dictate the construction work that would be carried out on the pool.

“These works will be laid out by our revised scope works. As we speak, our council officers are working on that reviewed plan and we hope to have it done by the end of the month,” said Mr Rasoki.

He said the council had yet to receive any word from the Ministry of Local Government of any plans for the funding of the leftover works.

“All we have been asked to do by the ministry was to revise the scope of work which we are doing at the moment. We have a consultant that we are working closely with who is looking at the overall plan of the construction work and looking at every detail and the different stages that we need to go through to complete the project.

“Again, I have to reiterate that the council from the very beginning has been the facilitator of this project.”

Mr Rasoki added discussions on the original plans for the project such as establishing an international standard swimming pool has yet to be revisited.

“The discussions about having an international standard swimming pool is quite controversial and when we came in, we inherited that.

“What we were told when we came in was to put that controversial side of the project aside, turn a new chapter and work towards completing it. The controversial side of the project was left to the other authorities like the ministry and FICAC.”

Questions sent to the ministry and FICAC on the status of investigations last month remained unanswered.

item.title: Rabuka defends inquiry spending
item.description: QUESTIONS over the value of public funds spent on the Commission of Inquiry have been dismissed by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka. He says the exercise has served its purpose despite some cases ending with no case to answer rulings or not guilty verdicts.
item.content:encoded:
QUESTIONS over the value of public funds spent on the Commission of Inquiry have been dismissed by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.

He says the exercise has served its purpose despite some cases ending with no case to answer rulings or not guilty verdicts.

“It is worth it, the very fact that people out there know that if they do something questionable, they will be subjected to investigative arms of the government,” he said.

Mr Rabuka maintained that the Commission of Inquiry’s role ended once it submitted its findings and recommendations, saying decisions on whether criminal charges should follow rested with prosecuting authorities.

“The report comes out as the report, it’s taken to the President, the President gives it to me, and I channel the report and the various recommendations on to the various branches that can prosecute.”

“The Commission of Inquiry does not prosecute.”

He said the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption and Police determined whether the report’s recommendations warranted further investigations or prosecutions.

“The credibility of the COI report and its recommendations will have to be determined by the court — if they recommend to investigate further and prosecute, if they find merits in prosecution.”

Mr Rabuka said some matters arising from the report had already been tested in court and dismissed. He also said the constitutional provisions governing FICAC would remain in force until amended through the constitutional process, including parliamentary approval and a national referendum.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | New $30m boiler for sugar mill
item.description: Back in May of 1994, The Fiji Times had reported that the Fiji Sugar Corporation was planning to undertake about $70 million worth of new projects over five years. Corporation chairman Lyle Cupit made the announcement while inspecting a newly commissioned $30 million boiler at the Lautoka mill.
item.content:encoded:
Back in May of 1994, The Fiji Times had reported that the Fiji Sugar Corporation was planning to undertake about $70 million worth of new projects over five years.

Corporation chairman Lyle Cupit made the announcement while inspecting a newly commissioned $30 million boiler at the Lautoka mill.

He said the corporation’s board would soon approve the new five-year plan with hopes of earning sufficient returns from the mills to finance the projects.

“With our present earnings, we might have to borrow money to implement the project, and this is causing concern,” Mr Cupit said.

He said the mill’s new multi-million Thomson boiler, which consisted of a 12-megawatt turbogenerator, a water treatment plant, and an upgraded electricity supply system, would be operational for the 1994 crushing season scheduled to start on June 7 of that year.

He said the boiler was the most modern available and should prove highly efficient and beneficial, and that the Lautoka mill would then operate with three boilers, and the other old, small Thomson boilers would be dismantled.

Mr Cupit said the board recognised steam and power-generating facilities had been a constraint to proper crushing operations at Lautoka, and that approval for the boiler had come in 1992 after a study by the corporation’s head office technical team.

He added that a $600,000 water treatment plant would hopefully curb water supply problems faced by the mill the previous season.

He revealed that since its inception, the corporation had spent over $235m on capital projects, with over $105m spent in the previous five years alone.

Mr Cupit said the corporation had the responsibility to ensure the continued viability of its factories and had continued to improve factory operations, increase crushing rates, shorten crushing seasons, and increase efficiency.

“With current pressure on the sugar industry in the world environment, changes will be necessary, including rationalisation of operations to ensure that the corporation remains competitive.”

Mr Cupit said the corporation looked forward to everyone’s support to make the 1994 crushing season a successful one.

He was accompanied on his tour by Lautoka mill general manager Ram Karan Singh, chief advising engineer John Korma, and factory manager William Thaggard.

item.title: Solar program extends coverage
item.description: A regional initiative to equip Pacific communities with practical renewable energy skills is continuing to expand after completing its third solar photovoltaic (PV) installation in Fiji. The Fiji Solar Scholars program has trained 14 participants from Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu to plan, install and manage basic solar PV systems, with graduates now applying their skills in community projects.
item.content:encoded:
A regional initiative to equip Pacific communities with practical renewable energy skills is continuing to expand after completing its third solar photovoltaic (PV) installation in Fiji.

The Fiji Solar Scholars program has trained 14 participants from Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu to plan, install and manage basic solar PV systems, with graduates now applying their skills in community projects.

The latest installation at the Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS) headquarters in Suva follows earlier projects at Yavulo Kindergarten in Sigatoka and the FCOSS Western Office in Lautoka.

The program was delivered in May this year by 350.org Pacific in partnership with the Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities to make renewable energy expertise more accessible to grassroots communities.

350.org Pacific and Caribbean program lead Fenton Lutunatabua said the initiative was designed to help communities respond to growing economic and climate challenges.

“Distributed solar energy has the potential to address the high cost of living, energy poverty, and disaster response needs,” he said.

Mr Lutunatabua said while Pacific leaders continued to advocate internationally for climate finance and a transition away from fossil fuels, communities could also take practical steps through locally managed renewable energy projects.
